190.title: The one who offers a leaf (9.11–9.25)
190.hook: a poor man brings the richest friend in the world a handful of flattened rice
190.howItsDone: In daily puja many Hindus offer flowers, tulsi or bilva leaves, fruit and water at the home shrine; Gita 9.26 is often recited to explain that what matters is the love, not the size of the offering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, raja-guhya, the royal secret: all beings rest in God, like wind in the sky. Your line was the secret. Today, what someone can bring to the one who holds everything.

A poor Brahmin, the one later tellings call Sudama, has barely enough to feed his family. As a boy he studied with Krishna. Now Krishna is a king in a golden city, and Sudama's wife begs him to visit his old friend. But what do you bring a king? He borrows a few handfuls of flattened rice and ties them in a corner of his worn cloth. At the palace, Krishna runs to hug him, washes his feet, and then notices the little bundle he's trying to hide. What's that you've brought me?
screen: `A POOR MAN. A KING FOR A FRIEND.` → `A HANDFUL OF FLATTENED RICE.` → `WHAT'S THAT YOU'VE BROUGHT ME?`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, Krishna takes the rice and eats it with delight, and he speaks words that are also a verse of the Gita, the one that crowns today's reading: whoever offers me with love a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, I accept that offering of love from the one whose heart is pure. Gita nine, twenty-six. Patram, pushpam, phalam, toyam. Nothing costly; anyone can find them. The verses before it build the scene. Krishna says fools look past him in human form, but great souls, verse fourteen says, are always singing about him, bowing, steady in their vows. He is the ritual and the offering, the fire and the ghee, verse sixteen. He is the father of the world, verse seventeen; the mother, the grandparent; the goal, the support, the lord, the witness, the home, the refuge, the friend. Verse twenty-two: to those who worship me alone, always united with me, I bring what they lack and protect what they have. So when the Lord of everything gets to name what he wants, he names a leaf. Not because the gift is big, but because the love is real. The word the verse leans on is bhakti: devotion, love turned toward God. And Sudama, the story says, walked home without having asked for anything, and found his hut had become a palace.

segments.voice: Hold something small in your open hands, a glass of water, a leaf, a flower, a piece of fruit, or simply picture one, and think of what you'd offer with it: thanks, a worry, a person you love. If you pray, you can offer it to God, as the verse says; if not, simply hold it with care, as if it were a gift.
Bhakti. Devotion, love turned toward God. Gita nine, twenty-six: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, offered with love, is accepted.
Your line: a leaf, a flower, water. Anyone, anywhere, can find something to offer. Until tomorrow.

191.title: "Whatever you do, offer it" (9.26–9.28)
191.hook: one verse turns eating, giving and every ordinary chore into worship
191.howItsDone: Many Hindus offer food to God before eating (naivedya) and receive it back as prasad, and many try to dedicate their daily work as an offering in the spirit of Gita 9.27.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti: the one who offers a leaf, and Sudama's handful of rice. Your line was a leaf, a flower, water. Today the offering gets much bigger.

In many Hindu kitchens, before anyone eats, a small portion is set aside, sometimes on a little plate in front of an image of Krishna or at the family shrine. A moment, maybe a verse. Then the food comes back to the table, and it isn't just lunch anymore. It's prasad, grace, a gift returned. A leaf is one thing. But what about the rest of the day? The dishes, the email, the commute, the argument about whose turn it is to take out the trash? Today, one verse takes all of it.
screen: `A PORTION SET ASIDE.` → `LUNCH BECOMES PRASAD.` → `WHAT ABOUT THE REST OF THE DAY?`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-seven: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever discipline you practice, Arjuna, do it as an offering to me. In Sanskrit it's a list with a drumbeat: yat karoshi, whatever you do; yad ashnasi, whatever you eat; yaj juhoshi, whatever you offer into the fire; dadasi yat, whatever you give; yat tapasyasi, whatever effort you make. Five whatevers, and one instruction: tat kurushva mad-arpanam, make it an offering to me. Look at the list. It starts with doing, the most general thing, and the second item is eating. Not meditating, not reading scripture. Eating. The Gita puts lunch right next to sacrifice. Yesterday Krishna asked for a leaf. Today he asks for the whole day: not more stuff, more of your ordinary life, turned in a direction. Verse twenty-eight says what happens. You'll be freed from the bonds of action, with its good and bad fruits; with your mind set on this yoga of letting go, you'll be free, and you'll come to me. Some readers hear chapter three's work without attachment and chapter four's sacrifice coming together here. The easiest way to stop clutching the fruit of an action is to give it away before you start.

segments.voice: Walk through today's whatevers: one task you'll do, one meal you'll eat, one small thing you'll give, one hard moment of effort. For each, take a breath and imagine handing it over before it happens: this is offered. If you pray, you can offer it to Krishna, as the verse says.
Arpana. Offering, handing over. Gita nine, twenty-seven: whatever you do, eat, offer, give or strive for, make it an offering.
Your line: offer everything. Nothing in a day is too ordinary to offer. Day one hundred ninety-one, offered.

192.title: Even the worst (9.29–9.34)
192.hook: a highway robber becomes a poet; the Gita says the door was never locked
192.howItsDone: Many Hindus hold that devotion to God is open to everyone regardless of birth or past, and the story of Valmiki, the robber who became the poet of the Ramayana, is widely told to show that anyone can turn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, arpana: whatever you do, eat, give or strive for, make it an offering. Your line was offer everything. Today, the end of chapter nine.

Valmiki, the poet of the Ramayana, was once a highway robber, or so the story people tell goes, stopping travelers in the forest. One day he stopped a sage, who asked him a simple question: your family shares what you steal, but will they share the wrongs you did to get it? The robber went home and asked. They said no. He came back shaken, and the sage gave him the name of Rama to repeat. He sat repeating it so long that an anthill grew over him. And he came out a poet.
screen: `A ROBBER IN THE FOREST.` → `WILL YOUR FAMILY SHARE THE WRONG?` → `HE CAME OUT A POET.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-nine: I am the same to all beings. No one is hateful to me, and no one is my favorite. But those who worship me with love are in me, and I am in them. Then verse thirty, the one that surprises people: even if someone of very bad conduct worships me with undivided devotion, they should be considered good, because they've made the right resolve. Not good eventually. Good now, because of which way they've turned. Verse thirty-one: quickly they become righteous and reach lasting peace. And Krishna tells Arjuna to announce it: my devotee never perishes. Na me bhaktah pranashyati. Verse thirty-two widens the circle. Those who take refuge in me, even those the society of the time held low, women, merchants and farmers, laborers, reach the highest goal. The verse names groups the ranking of its day placed below others, and readers today argue about its wording; some find it painful, some read it as those groups being singled out for welcome. Some hear a widening: doors that were closed, pushed open. Verse thirty-four, the chapter's last, is the whole of it in a line: fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, offer to me, bow to me, and you'll come to me. In the Gita's telling, nobody is too far gone to turn.

segments.voice: Think of someone you've written off: someone who hurt you, a public figure, maybe a younger version of yourself. You don't have to excuse anything they did; just hold them for a moment in the light of verse thirty, that turning is always possible. Breathe in and picture the door open; breathe out and let a little of the hardness go.
Bhakta. Devotee, one who loves God. Gita nine, thirty: whoever turns with undivided devotion, whatever they've done, is to be counted good. No one is outside.
Your line: no one is outside. The door stays open to anyone who turns. Chapter nine, complete.

193.title: The source (10.1–10.11)
193.hook: even the gods don't know where Krishna comes from, because he's where they come from
193.tomorrow: Arjuna asks: how do I think of you? (10.12–10.18)
193.howItsDone: Many Hindus gather for satsang, sitting together to sing and talk about God, which verse 10.9 describes as devotees awakening one another; Gita 10.8 is often recited for its picture of God as the source of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakta: even the worst, turned toward God, is counted good. Your line was no one is outside. Today, chapter ten opens.

Stand where a great river meets the sea. It's a mile wide, brown and slow, carrying whole trees. Now follow it back: past the cities, past the villages, into the hills, until it's a stream you could step across, then a trickle between two rocks, then a single spring, water rising out of the ground. Everything downstream came from there. Pilgrims make the long climb into the mountains just to stand at the Ganga's source. Chapter ten of the Gita begins by walking everything back to its source.
screen: `A RIVER A MILE WIDE.` → `FOLLOW IT BACK.` → `A SINGLE SPRING.`

segments.voice: Krishna says he'll speak again, because Arjuna delights in hearing. Verse two: neither the gods nor the great sages know my origin, because I am the origin of the gods and the sages, in every way. You can't find the source of the source by going upstream. Then a list that's easy to rush past. Understanding, knowledge, clear sight. Patience, truth, self-control, calm. Pleasure and pain. Birth and death. Fear and fearlessness. Nonviolence, evenness, contentment, discipline, generosity, fame and disgrace. All these states of beings, verse five says, come from me alone. Notice that pain and fear are on the list. The Gita doesn't hand the hard things to someone else. Verse eight: I am the source of all; from me everything moves. Knowing this, the wise worship me, full of feeling. Verse nine is almost a picture of a good evening with friends: their minds on me, their lives given to me, they awaken one another, always talking about me, content and full of joy. Bodhayantah parasparam: waking each other up. Verse ten: to those always united with me, who worship with love, I give the yoga of understanding by which they come to me. And verse eleven: out of compassion for them, living in their hearts, I destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge. Everything, even the hard things, flows from one spring.
screen: `THE ORIGIN OF THE GODS.` · `EVEN PAIN AND FEAR COME FROM ME.` · `WAKING EACH OTHER UP.` · `THE LAMP IN THE HEART.` · then, large: `I AM THE ORIGIN.`

segments.voice: Follow your breath back to its source: the air in the room, then the plants, oceans and sky behind it, one breath at a time, as far back as you can go. Then let the chain go and rest, as if sitting beside a spring. If you pray, you can hold verse eight in mind: from you, everything moves.
The source. Gita ten, eight: Krishna says he is the origin of all, and from him everything moves.
Your line: I am the origin. Friends who talk about what matters can wake each other up. See you tomorrow.

194.title: Arjuna asks: how do I think of you? (10.12–10.18)
194.hook: Arjuna believes every word, and still asks the most practical question in the book
194.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep God in mind through particular forms and places: an image at the home shrine, a sacred river, a tree, a name repeated through the day, in the spirit of Arjuna's question in Gita 10.17.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the source: everything flows from one spring. Your line was I am the origin. Today, Arjuna has a question.

Someone tells you something enormous. The ocean is two miles deep here. The universe is expanding. Your grandmother loved you more than anyone ever will. You believe it, you really do. Then you go and make a sandwich, and you have no idea how to hold that fact while spreading the mustard. Believing a thing and living with it are different skills. Arjuna has just heard that Krishna is the source of everything. He believes it. And then he asks the most practical question in the Gita: okay, but how do I actually think of you?
screen: `SOMETHING ENORMOUS.` → `THEN YOU MAKE A SANDWICH.` → `HOW DO I THINK OF YOU?`

segments.voice: Verse twelve is Arjuna's confession of faith. You are the highest Brahman, the highest home, the highest purifier, the eternal divine person, the first god, unborn, all-pervading. All the sages say so, he adds: Narada, Asita and Devala, Vyasa. And now you say it yourself. Verse fourteen: I accept everything you've told me as true. Neither the gods nor the demons know your full manifestation. Verse fifteen: only you know yourself, by yourself, highest person, source of beings, god of gods, lord of the world. A complete statement of belief. Verse sixteen asks: tell me, without leaving anything out, your divine glories, vibhutis, the powers by which you fill all these worlds. And verse seventeen: how shall I know you, master of yoga, by constant meditation? In which things, in which forms, should I think of you? It's a humble question, and a smart one. I can't think about everything at once. Give me some handles. Where do I look? Verse eighteen shows how he feels: tell me again, in detail. I never get tired of hearing your words; they're like nectar. So chapter ten isn't a list for its own sake. It answers a person who believes, and wants to know where to put their eyes on an ordinary day. Tomorrow comes the list. Today, the question.
screen: `YOU ARE THE HIGHEST BRAHMAN.` · `I ACCEPT IT ALL AS TRUE.` · `IN WHICH THINGS SHOULD I THINK OF YOU?` · `TELL ME AGAIN. IT'S NECTAR.` · then, large: `WHERE DO I LOOK?`

segments.voice: Ask Arjuna's question in your own way: where in your ordinary day is it easiest to notice something sacred, or something bigger than you? Maybe first light through a window, a child laughing, the first sip of tea, a piece of music. Let one answer come, and stay with it for the rest of the sit as your handle.
Arjuna asks. After believing it all, he asks: in which things should I think of you? Give me something to hold.
Your line: how to hold it. Believing is one skill; living with it takes a handle. That's day one hundred ninety-four.

195.title: "I am the taste in water" (10.19–10.42)
195.hook: Krishna answers Arjuna with a list: the best of every kind of thing, and one entry nobody expects
195.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor the presences named in Gita chapter ten: they bathe in the Ganga, circle the sacred fig tree, chant Om and repeat a divine name (japa), seeing each as a glimpse of the divine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna asked: in which things should I think of you? Your line was how to hold it. Today, Krishna answers, with a long list.

Pour a glass of cold water on a hot day and take a long drink. That exact clean taste when you're thirsty. Back in chapter seven, Krishna said: I am the taste in water. Not the water. The taste, the part you can't hold in your hand, that makes water water. Now Arjuna has asked where to look for him, and Krishna answers with a whole list built the same way: the best, the brightest, the deepest of every kind of thing. And somewhere in the middle, one entry that makes people stop and read it twice.
screen: `A LONG DRINK ON A HOT DAY.` → `NOT THE WATER. THE TASTE.` → `A LIST OF THE BEST OF EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: He begins at the center. Verse twenty: I am the self seated in the heart of all beings, their beginning, their middle and their end. Then the list. Among lights, I am the radiant sun. Among bodies of water, the ocean. Among words, the single syllable Om. Among offerings, the quiet repetition of a sacred name. Among things that stand still, the Himalaya. Among trees, the sacred fig. Among rivers, the Ganga. Among letters, the letter A, the first sound. Among seasons, spring, full of flowers. And, verse thirty-three, I am time that never runs out. Now the surprise. Verse thirty-six: I am the gambling of cheats. Wait, what? Commentators read it more than one way. One reading: Krishna is naming whatever is the most intense of its kind, even the kind no one would choose; whatever grips hardest has a spark of his power in it. Then, verse thirty-seven, a wink: among the Pandavas, I am Arjuna. He names the very man he's talking to. Verse forty-one gives the rule for the whole list: whatever is glorious, beautiful, or mighty, know that it springs from a spark of my splendor. And the last verse: but what do you need all this detail for, Arjuna? I hold up this entire universe with a single fragment of myself. So the list is a set of handles, things you meet every day: the taste in water, the sun, the letter A.

segments.voice: Take one slow sip of water, or remember the last time you drank when you were really thirsty, and stay with the taste: the cool, the clean, the relief. Then let your attention move to the light, a sound, the air on your skin, and notice what's best in each. If you pray, you can hold verse forty-one in mind: every glory is a spark.
Rasa. Taste, flavor, essence, the part you can't hold in your hand that makes water water. Krishna's handles for the sacred: the best of each kind, every glory a spark of his splendor.
Your line: in everything. Even a sip of water can be a handle. On to chapter eleven tomorrow.

196.title: Arjuna asks to see (11.1–11.8)
196.hook: hearing isn't enough; Arjuna asks to see God's real form, and is told his eyes won't do
196.howItsDone: Many Hindus speak of darshan, seeing and being seen by the divine, when they visit a temple; chapter eleven, where Arjuna asks to see and is given a divine eye, is often read as the Gita's great darshan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rasa: I am the taste in water, and a list of glories that ended in a single spark. Your line was in everything. Today, the end of the week, and chapter eleven begins.

Love someone who lives far away, and a moment can come: the calls are wonderful, the letters are wonderful, and at some point you just say, I need to see you. Arjuna has listened for ten chapters. This week alone: the one who offers a leaf; whatever you do, offer it; even the worst, and no one is outside; the source; how to think of God; the taste in water. A week of hearing. That's where chapter eleven starts.
screen: `I NEED TO SEE YOU.` → `A WEEK OF HEARING.` → `CHAPTER ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Verse one: out of kindness to me you've told me this highest secret about the self, and my confusion is gone. Verse two: I've heard in detail how beings come and go, and about your greatness that doesn't end. Verse three: it is just as you say. But I want to see it: your form as the Lord of all. Then verse four, a lovely bit of humility: if you think I'm able to see it, master of yoga, show me your imperishable self. If you think I'm able. He doesn't demand. He asks, and leaves room for no. Krishna says yes. Verse five: behold my forms, by hundreds and thousands, divine, of many colors and shapes. Verse six: see the gods of the sky and the storm, the twin healers, wonders no one has seen before. Verse seven: see the whole universe, moving and unmoving, gathered here in my body, and anything else you want to see. Then the catch, verse eight: you can't see me with these eyes of yours, so I give you a divine eye. Divyam chakshuh. Behold my power. That's the key to the whole chapter. Seeing God isn't a matter of looking harder with ordinary eyes; the sight itself has to be given. In the Mahabharata, the narrator Sanjaya, telling all this to the blind king, has been given a divine eye too, so he can see the battlefield from the palace. That's how anyone hearing the story gets to watch.

segments.voice: Close your eyes and notice that everything you usually look at is gone, yet something is still seeing: shapes, colors, the dark behind the lids. Rest in that. Then think of one thing, or one person, you'd like to see more truly, and without forcing anything, ask in your own way, as Arjuna did: if I'm able, show me.
Divyam chakshuh. A divine eye. After hearing, Arjuna asks for sight, and Krishna gives him this eye, because ordinary eyes can't see it.
Your line: show me. Arjuna asked, and left room for no. A whole week, done.

original.note: Sanskrit: divyam chakshuh, a divine eye (11.8); chakshuh, the eye, the power of seeing.

trapdoor: what you thought: if God were real, you'd just see it.
what it means: ordinary eyes can't see it; the sight has to be given, and Arjuna asks humbly, if you think I'm able.
what a scholar hears: the Gita is framed as Sanjaya's report to the blind king Dhritarashtra, made possible by divine sight granted by Vyasa; 11.8 grants Arjuna the same kind of sight.
